geis.json.text: A geis is a ritual prohibition in early Irish literature, and the plural is gessa. The word names a taboo or sworn injunction that binds a named person, most often a king or a hero. Scholars link it to the verb guidid, 'prays' or 'asks', so the taboo began as a formal request. Welsh gwŷs, 'summons', may come from the same Common Celtic formation. Irish texts also use other words for the same idea, among them airmit and airgart. No court or lawman enforced geasa. The narrative holds that gods, the heroic code, or unnamed cosmic powers made them bite. Most gessa came at birth or when a person took up a new role, so breaking one undid that person's own nature. The tales use the pattern to mark a hero's doom in advance. King Conaire Mór of Tara carried a string of prohibitions: no hunting of the birds of the air, no night away from Tara, no entry by three red riders. He broke them one by one, and the breaking led to his death in Togail Bruidne Da Derga. Some scholars think the idea came from the Bible, while others argue for a native Irish institution. A Welsh parallel appears in the swearing of destiny in the Welsh tales Math and Culhwch ac Olwen. The concept joined magical force to social duty, and it shaped how storytellers built a hero's rise and fall.

attributes.attribute: is a ritual taboo that binds a named king or hero
was enforced by gods or cosmic powers, not by courts
is linked etymologically to the verb guidid, 'prays, asks'
has a Welsh counterpart in the swearing of destiny
broke his gessa and met death at Da Derga's hostel

okr.objective: Explain the Irish ritual prohibition called geis, its origin, its enforcement, and its narrative work.
key_results: Define geis and its plural gessa as a binding taboo.
Give the proposed etymology from guidid and the Welsh cognate gwŷs.
Show how Conaire Mór's broken gessa drive the plot of Togail Bruidne Da Derga.
Compare the Irish concept with the Welsh swearing of destiny.

Goibniu.json.text: Goibniu is the Irish smith god, one of the Tuatha Dé Danann's craft masters. He forged a working silver arm for King Nuada after the battle took his own, though some versions give that deed to Dian Cécht. A king with a blemish had to step down, so Bres took the throne. Lebar Gabála Érenn lists Goibniu beside Luichne the carpenter, Créidne the metalworker, and Dian Cécht the healer. Lost law tracts carried his name, among them Bretha Goibnenn. The three craftsmen work side by side in Cath Maige Tuired to turn out swords, spears, and javelins for the war against the Fomoiri. Ruadán, son of Bres and Bríg, comes to kill him and wounds him, but Goibniu drives a spear through the young man. Ruadán's mother then invented keening, the wild sound of grief. The Early Modern tale Altromh Tige Dá Medar says the feast of Goibniu kept the Tuath Dé free of age and death. His cauldron's guests drank and grew younger. He healed his wounds at a sacred well on Slane hill, owned the wonder cow Glas Gaibhleann, and was tied to County Cavan. Modern folklore remembers him as Gobbán Saor, the skilled mason. His Welsh counterpart is Gofannon fab Dôn, and both names descend from an old word for smith.

okr.objective: Present Goibniu as the Irish smith god, his craft, his kin, and his afterlife in folklore.
key_results: Place Goibniu among the craft gods of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
Record the silver arm, the killing of Ruadán, and the deathless feast.
Link him to the lost Bretha Goibnenn and to Gofannon fab Dôn.
Show his survival as Gobbán Saor in modern tradition.

Gebrinius.json.text: Gebrinius, also called Mercurius Gebrinius, is a Continental Celtic deity known from ten inscriptions and a second-century shrine, all at Bonn in Germany. The Romans set him beside Mars in their warrior pantheon. Most of the record comes from the Ubii, a people of eastern Gaul, so the god may belong to a frontier zone where Celtic and Germanic worship met. The meaning of the epithet is not settled. One reading points to a horned god and compares Old Irish gabor and Welsh gafr, both meaning 'goat'. No firm parallel supports that view. Images show a creature with a lion-like head on a body closer to a fat sheep. The small corpus and the single cult place leave his character open.

attributes.attribute: is attested by ten inscriptions and a 2nd-century shrine at Bonn
was equated with Mars by Roman worshippers
may take his epithet from a word for goat
is shown with a lion-like head and a sheep-like body

okr.objective: Document Gebrinius as a poorly attested Continental deity of the Rhine frontier.
key_results: Fix the cult place at Bonn and the count of ten inscriptions.
Record the Roman equation with Mars and the title Mercurius Gebrinius.
State the disputed 'goat' etymology and the animal iconography.

Grail.json.text: The Holy Grail is a symbolic object pictured as the sacred cup Jesus drank from at the Last Supper. Some tellings describe it as the platter for his bread or the paschal lamb. Others say it caught his blood as he lay dying. Joseph of Arimathea, the merchant who owned the supper house, carried the Grail to Britain. The Christian emblem of transubstantiation then fused with Celtic legends into a complex tale that still moves poets and thinkers. In that tale the Fisher King lies wounded in his body and heals only when the quest is complete. Celtic studies reads the Grail at two levels. The first asks whether older Celtic vessels lie behind it. Loomis and others point to wonder cauldrons that feed or revive: the peir dadeni of Branwen, the chief of Annwn's cauldron in Preiddiau Annwfn, and Diwrnach's vessel in Culhwch ac Olwen. The pearl-rimmed cauldron of the poem will not boil meat for a coward or a liar, a moral test close to the Grail's own. Cauldrons placed in lakes and bogs, as at Llyn Fawr, show that such vessels held ritual weight in Late Bronze and Iron Age deposits. Other scholars read the severed head of the Welsh procession as a trace of the Celtic head cult. The second level is the later Welsh and Irish retelling of French Grail romances.

attributes.attribute: is imagined as the cup of the Last Supper and the vessel of Christ's blood
may descend from Celtic cauldrons of plenty and rebirth
serves as a moral test that only the worthy knight can pass
is healed only when the Grail quest succeeds

okr.objective: Set out the Holy Grail as a Christian symbol with Celtic antecedents and a long literary afterlife.
key_results: Record the cup, platter, and blood-vessel forms of the Grail.
Name the Celtic cauldrons proposed as forerunners.
Explain the moral test shared by cauldron and Grail.
Note the Welsh and Irish adaptations of French romances.

Gaul.json.text: Gaul was an ancient Celtic land. It covers lands now part of France. It also included areas of modern Belgium, Germany, and Switzerland. In Roman usage the name means the region bounded by the Rhine, the Alps, the Mediterranean, the Pyrenees, the Atlantic, and the English Channel. The narrower term Gallia Transalpina, Gaul beyond the Alps, marks it off from Cisalpine Gaul in northern Italy. Lepontic inscriptions show that Celtic speech was already present in northern Italy by the sixth century BCE or earlier. Roman writers such as Livy tell of settlers coming from beyond the Alps in the fifth century. The Po valley became a base for raids south, including the sack of Rome around 390 BCE, until Rome won at Telamon in 225 BCE. Julius Caesar brought the northern lands under Roman power. He wrote about them in his Gallic Wars. Much of what we know about continental Celts comes from Caesar. His truthfulness is hard to gauge. He wanted political power over the Celts. The Gauls were not one tribe. They were many tribal peoples. They shared a speech and broadly similar beliefs and customs. The Latin Gallia meant 'land of the Galli', and the same root appears in Greek Galatai, the name of the settlers of Galatia.

attributes.attribute: is bounded by the Rhine, Alps, Mediterranean, Pyrenees, Atlantic, and Channel
is divided into Transalpine and Cisalpine regions
was subdued by Caesar in campaigns from 58 to 51 BCE

okr.objective: Define Gaul as a geographical and cultural term and trace its Roman conquest.
key_results: Give the physical bounds of Transalpine Gaul.

Galatia.json.text: Galatia was an ancient Celtic land. It stood in central Anatolia. That region is now part of Turkey. Celts settled there during the 3rd century BCE. Classical sources say the Gauls crossed into Phrygia in 278 BCE at the call of Nicomedes I, the Thracian ruler of Bithynia. They came in families, so the move looks like a migration and not a slow mixing of mercenaries. The incomers may have gathered survivors of the Celtic invasion of Greece under Brennos. Three tribes held the land: the Tolistobogii in the west, the Tectosages around Ancyra, and the Trocmi in the east. They kept their Galatian speech and many Celtic customs for centuries under Roman rule. They met at a sacred oak grove called Drunemeton. Four tetrarchs governed, three of them military, and the fourth served as a judge, perhaps a druid. St. Paul mentioned the region in his epistles. He wrote to the residents of the land, but the community he addressed may have been largely non-Celtic and taken its name from Galatian neighbours.

attributes.attribute: was settled by Gauls in 278 BCE
held the Tolistobogii, Tectosages, and Trocmi tribes
kept the Galatian language under Roman rule
had a sacred oak assembly called Drunemeton

okr.objective: Describe Galatia as a Celtic land in Anatolia, its tribes, institutions, and language.
key_results: Date the Galatian settlement to 278 BCE under Nicomedes I.
Name the three tribes and their chief centres.
Record Drunemeton and the fourfold tetrarchy.
Qualify St. Paul's address to the Galatians.

Gundestrup_Cauldron.json.text: The Gundestrup Cauldron is a great silver vessel of the old world. Peat cutters found it in May 1891 in Rævemosen, a bog beside the hamlet of Gundestrup in Himmerland, northern Jutland, Denmark. Within two days the crown claimed it as treasure trove, and it went to the Danish National Museum. Someone had placed it in the marsh, perhaps as an offering to the gods or to hide it in danger. The bowl has thirteen silver plates, several of them partly gilded. Scholars date the bowl to the second or first century before the common era, though the date is still argued. Many call the vessel a Celtic work. The technique and style point to Thrace: animal fur is picked out with punch marks, and the silver is heavily beaten. The motifs are Celtic all the same, with Celtic helmets and carnyces, the long battle trumpets. The Cimbri may have carried it north on their raid. Figures in relief show a goddess on a cart, a horned god, a wheel-bearing bearded man, and an antlered god holding a torc and a ram-headed snake. One plate shows warriors led toward a large figure who dips a man into a vessel. That scene recalls the cauldron of rebirth in the Branwen tale, and it may picture a rite of initiation or sacrifice. The images echo the ones the Celts knew in other lands.

attributes.attribute: was found in a Danish bog in May 1891
is made of thirteen partly gilded silver plates
joins Thracian technique to Celtic motifs
shows a scene of immersion that may mean rebirth

okr.objective: Report the discovery, manufacture, and iconography of the Gundestrup Cauldron.
key_results: Fix the find place and date in northern Jutland.
Describe the thirteen silver plates and their mixed style.
Name the main divine figures and the immersion scene.
Connect the vessel to Celtic cauldron myth.

Glastonbury.json.text: Glastonbury is a British mythological site. Some regard the small southwestern English city as the location of Avalon, the Otherworld island. Ruins of Christian buildings lie below the pyramidal Tor. Glastonbury Abbey once stood there, and legend buries King Arthur and Queen Guinevere beneath it. The Chalice Well, also named Blood Spring, holds iron-red water. Joseph of Arimathea is said to have raised Britain's first Christian church. Legend also names Glastonbury a doorway to Annwn, the realm ruled by Gwynn ap Nudd, king of the fairies. Iron Age settlement on the Tor marks its ancient past. Archaeology fills in the longer story. Neolithic people built timber and brushwood trackways across the Somerset Levels, and the Sweet Track was dated by tree rings to the winter of 3807–3806 BCE. The Meare Heath trackway shows that work on the same scale continued in the second millennium BCE. Arthur Bulleid's late nineteenth-century digs uncovered an Iron Age lake village at the marsh edge. Roman finds are modest, though pottery and tiles hint at a villa near the later abbey. Beckery was a small medieval daughter-house of the abbey. The bank called Ponter's Ball bank up to ten metres wide and three and a half metres high, runs for about a kilometre toward the town, and its purpose is still debated.

okr.objective: Cover Glastonbury as both a mythic site and a deeply stratified archaeological landscape.
key_results: Keep the Avalon, Arthur, and Chalice Well traditions.

__new__Gofannon.name: Gofannon fab Dôn
__new__Gofannon.text: Gofannon fab Dôn is a smith god of early Welsh tradition and a son of Dôn. His name joins Welsh gof, 'smith', to a divine suffix, and it is related to but not the same as the Irish name Goibniu. Modern writers often treat the two as cognate craft gods. In Culhwch ac Olwen, the giant Ysbaddaden sets Culhwch the task of sharpening the iron tools of Amaethon, and Gofannon must do the work. In Math fab Mathonwy he kills Dylan, the strange sea-born child of his sister Arianrhod. A poem in Llyfr Taliesin names Caer Gofannon, the god's stronghold. Another poem speaks of the seven spears of Gofannon, so he was remembered as a maker of famous weapons. A mould from Corbridge on Hadrian's Wall shows a smith god with tongs and a hammer above an anvil, and this image fits the Romano-British setting of such craft deities. His story survives in fragments, but it places a divine craftsman inside the family of Dôn and the older mythic layer of Welsh literature.

__new__Grannus.name: Grannus
__new__Grannus.text: Grannus, or Apollo Grannus, is a Gaulish god whom Roman worshippers joined to Apollo. The pairing belongs to interpretatio romana, the habit of matching Celtic gods with Greek and Roman ones. He was a healer, and people sought his help across the empire. Eighteen inscriptions name him. In only one, from Bonn, is he called Grannus alone. Elsewhere the name serves as a byname of Apollo. Offerings to him appear in the Rhineland, at Musselburgh near Edinburgh, at Brigetio in Hungary, at Astorga in Spain, in Västmanland in Sweden, and at Ephesus in Turkey. The German city of Aachen was known as Aquis Granni, 'the waters of Grannus', which points to a sacred spring of Romano-Celtic date. His female partner was Sirona, whose name means something like 'star goddess' and is surely Celtic. The meaning of Grannus is less clear. A link to Irish grian, 'sun', might explain why Apollo fits, and the Irish heroine Gráinne has been proposed as a further cognate.

okr.objective: Document Grannus as a Gaulish healing god of the Roman period.
key_results: Explain his equation with Apollo under interpretatio romana.

__new__Glewlwyd.name: Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr
__new__Glewlwyd.text: Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr is a gatekeeper in Welsh Arthurian literature. He first appears in a dialogue poem that asks, 'Who is the gatekeeper?' (Pa Gur yv y Porthaur?). There he stubbornly refuses entry to Arthur, Cai, and a crowd of the best men in the world. The prose Culhwch ac Olwen reverses his role. He bars the gate of Arthur's court at Celliwig against Culhwch, then goes inside and praises the young man to Arthur in a long and boastful speech. The poem hints that Glewlwyd held the gate only on three high festivals, and that deputies took his place at other times. His epithet suggests that guarding the gate was his fixed office. He does not appear in Chrétien de Troyes's Yvain or Erec et Enide, and his place in the Welsh romances marks a native figure pushing back into plots borrowed from French. His stand at the door has a close Irish parallel: the gatekeeper Camall mac Rágail first denies Lug entry at Tara in Cath Maige Tuired.

okr.objective: Present Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr as the Welsh Arthurian gatekeeper and his literary setting.
key_results: Name Pa Gur yv y Porthaur? as the earliest text.

__new__Gwenhwyfar.name: Gwenhwyfar
__new__Gwenhwyfar.text: Gwenhwyfar is the wife of Arthur in Welsh tradition. French and English forms of her name include Guenevere, Guinevere, and Guenièvre, and Latin texts of Geoffrey of Monmouth give Guenhuuera and Guanhumara. She stands in the earliest stratum of Arthurian story, beside Cai, Bedwyr, Medrawd, Celliwig's court, and Caledfwlch the sword. In Culhwch ac Olwen, Arthur counts her among his prized possessions and will not give her up, and the tale names her chief of the queens of this island. Triad 56 calls Arthur's three great queens by her name alone. The theme of her abduction comes first in Caradog of Llancarfan's twelfth-century Life of Gildas, where Melwas carries her off, and the dialogue poem of Melwas and Gwenhwyfar rests on the same story. Historia Regum Britanniae has her forced to marry the usurper Modred while Arthur is away. One triad blames a quarrel between her and her sister Gwenhwyfach for the battle of Camlan, and another lists her among the faithless wives. The later romances give the triangle its familiar shape with Lancelot. Her name matches Old Irish Findabair, from find, 'white', and siabair, 'phantom'.

key_results: List the name variants and the oldest Arthurian core.
